Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA View image in fullscreen The AfD has launched a ‘think German’ campaign that promises promising a ‘new, patriotic cultural policy’ and an end to funding for ‘anti-German art and culture’. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA Germany The Nazis drove Bauhaus out of town. Now the far right is waging another war against the movement Poll to take place in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, where Bauhaus blossomed a century ago – and where AfD is promising ‘patriotic culture policy’ if it wins Deborah Cole in Dessau-Roßlau Thu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The city of Dessau, where the Bauhaus design school flourished a century ago, catapulted Germany into the modern era and revolutionised global design. It is also where the Nazis drove the avant garde movement out of town and attempted to crush its utopian principles. A hundred years later, another high-stakes culture war over its legacy is looming. The EU’s biggest democracy will face one of the riskiest tests of the postwar period when Dessau’s home state of Saxony-Anhalt goes to the polls on 6 September. In what would be a first since Adolf Hitler’s time, a far-right party could win an absolute majority and take power in one of the 16 Länder . View image in fullscreen An Alternative for Germany (AfD) party rally in Dessau, Germany. The AfD is running first in national polls and poised to capture about 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. Photograph: Maryam Majd/Reuters The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is running first in national polls and is poised to capture about 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. It has widened its double-digit lead among the state’s 1.8 million voters by homing in on the cost of living, fears around immigration, and the whipsaw effects of deindustrialisation and depopulation. But the party’s programme also lays out a vision for Germany with Saxony-Anhalt as a foothold, in a plan oddly fixated on Bauhaus. “The state government is running an image campaign called ‘think modern’ that seeks to derive the identity of Saxony-Anhalt from Bauhaus,” reads one passage. The AfD said it is countering with “a ‘think German’ campaign” that promises a “new, patriotic cultural policy” and an end to funding for “anti-German art and culture”. Bauhaus’s blend of form and function in architecture, art and industrial design shaped everything from Ikea style for the masses to the user-friendly elegance of Apple products. It was also a buzzing hive of sexual liberation, new roles for women and international collaboration before the Nazis drove its “degenerates” into exile. View image in fullscreen The director of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, Barbara Steiner, says the AfD’s anti-Bauhaus crusade is a Trojan horse aiming for the heart of Germany’s open, liberal society. Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News. In her modest, sleek-lined office at the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, director Barbara Steiner said that much like a century ago, the AfD’s anti-Bauhaus crusade was a Trojan horse aiming for the heart of Germany’s open, liberal society. “There would be a lot of people leaving the state”, if the AfD took control, said the Austrian-born Steiner. She argued the region was underestimated by its purported champions and their “absurd” war on a warped vision of Bauhaus. “People are always talking about the economic downturn and how everything’s going down the drain, but the people here are brilliant,” she said. “I’m afraid what is now so tenderly sprouting will be snuffed out by this rigidity and isolation.” While her own institution would probably face funding cuts, her bigger worries concern the chilling effects on public debate, cooperation and innovation. “They want cultural hegemony. That’s the really threatening thing.” Today Dessau-Roßlau, as the city has been known since a municipal consolidation in 2007, can seem like an open-air museum of the past 100 years’ tumult. Its historic, deserted market square is bookended by soaring spires. But taller still are the prefab communist-era housing blocks hulking over gutted brick warehouses. And on nearly every lamp-post, an AfD poster hangs with the promise “Our Year”. View image in fullscreen The Bauhaus Dessau, a Unesco world heritage site designed by Walter Gropius and built between 1925 and 1926. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters The sprawling Bauhaus campus and a glass-and-steel museum which opened in 2019 attract tens of thousands of visitors each year. But city authorities say tourism will never lift the economy out of the doldrums. Unemployment sits at 10%, against 8% across the state and 6% at the national level. Household income in Saxony-Anhalt falls near the bottom of the German table. With an average age above 50 , Dessau-Roßlau is one of the country’s most geriatric cities. Its population has shrunk to 75,000 from 130,000 in 1990, the year Germany reunified, driven by an exodus led by highly educated young women. View image in fullscreen The Bauhaus-influenced 1930s modernist Isokon apartment building, in Hampstead, London. The Bauhaus movement catapulted Germany into the modern era and revolutionised global design. Photograph: UrbanImages/Alamy The 13-year-old AfD has said it wants to repopulate Saxony-Anhalt using lavish family subsidies with unclear financing, while freeing up lost potential by “liberating” Germans from shame over the Holocaust . Authorities classify the national party as suspected extremist and the Saxony-Anhalt chapter as confirmed extremist, meaning it poses a threat to democracy. Its flag-bearer is Ulrich Siegmund, a telegenic regional MP with reported ties to known neo-Nazis . Siegmund attended an infamous meeting in November 2023 to discuss a “remigration” plan for mass deportations. View image in fullscreen An election campaign billboard that shows Saxony-Anhalt premier Sven Schulze of the Christian Democratic Union and reads: ‘Listen. Understand. Do.’ Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty Images At a candidates’ debate on Dessau’s outskirts, the mainstream parties pleaded with voters to consider the consequences of backing the AfD. Making his pitch, state premier, Sven Schulze, of the Christian Democratic Union, the party of Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , did not make a single reference to the historically unpopular leader. Schulze, the only candidate with a chance of standing in the way of the AfD, has often seemed to be campaigning against his own party, most recently attacking a signature national pension reform plan. He accused the AfD of selling snake oil on growth, jobs and borders. “Even if the day after tomorrow all women decide they’re only there for baby-making, as some (parties) seem to want, that won’t solve the problem,” he said. “It’s important to be honest: we will also need people from abroad in the coming years, particularly in the care sector and in hospitals.” Tobias Rausch, in the state parliament for the AfD since 2016, brushed off questions about the legality of its calls for mass expulsions of asylum seekers. “We want to rescue the country from politicians from the old parties and finally make policies for the people,” he said. “We don’t just want to change things in Saxony-Anhalt but also at the national level.” Armin Willingmann, a veteran Social Democrat struggling to keep Germany’s oldest party in the regional parliament, appealed to a sense of pride in regional accomplishments, including Bauhaus. “This is a place of exceptional cultural significance – our global culture,” he said. “We really must be careful not to shut the door, not to adopt Herr Rausch’s quite crude policy of isolationism.” Undecided voters said they appreciated local patriotism but that the politicians seemed to be talking past economic realities. View image in fullscreen Local voters Ruth Schulze and Maria Karius. Photograph: Deborah Cole/The Guardian “If the economy is blossoming here, why is there no money to be found anywhere?” said Ruth Schulze, in her 60s and no relation to the CDU candidate. “I was born and bred in Dessau and don’t want to speak ill of it – but the lack of money really is the number one issue,” said Schulze, who runs an advertising agency she said was struggling with overhead costs. Teacher Maria Karius, 40, said the far right had come to be seen as a normal part of the political landscape as frustration with the mainstream parties festered. Despite a 15-% drop in the Dessau crime rate last year, she said there was a perception that public spaces weren’t safe. “Nothing changes – it’s always the same. That’s fertile ground for the AfD.” While the debate’s tone often sounded resigned, back in town there were still some echoes of Bauhaus’s revolutionary esprit. View image in fullscreen Rima Al Ahmad describes the shared community space she shares with other artists as a kind of resistance against her state’s increasingly ‘notorious’ image. Photograph: Deborah Cole/The Guardian Rima Al Ahmad, who came to Dessau from the bigger city of Halle a decade ago to study design, works in a shared community space for artists and creators called Vor Ort, which translates as on site or local. It was conceived of as a “cultural anchor” for German and international students drawn to courses rooted in Bauhaus traditions. “It can be hard to find your place here if you come from outside,” she said. On a tour of its printmaking workshop, recording studio and lush community garden, Al Ahmad, 32, born to a Syrian father and a German mother, described the project as a kind of resistance against her state’s increasingly “notorious” image. “I was born in Saxony-Anhalt and for me, Saxony-Anhalt is home,” she said. “It has beautiful places and great, just normal people, regardless of the far right.” Asked what the Bauhaus pioneers would think of Vor Ort, she smiled: “I think they’d like that the experimental spirit is being carried forward here.” Explore more on these topics Germany Bauhaus The far right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A three-year-old girl has died after a visit to a petting zoo triggered a bacterial infection, prompting health authorities to raise the alarm about the rare but potentially fatal syndrome, AAP reports. Sassi died in a Melbourne hospital after developing Haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, known as HUS, seven weeks after a trip to a petting zoo where she held, rode and petted animals, the Salter family said in a GoFundMe post. The family of four said they had “been living a nightmare” after the toddler spent six weeks in intensive care battling kidney failure and a brain injury. The family wrote: We’ve lost our darling girl. Sassi was strong. Surprising many at each corner. She was courageous and a fighter. She fought so hard. We all fought so hard. The child contracted a strain of the E.Coli bacteria (STEC) which releases toxins into the body, inflaming blood vessels and causing clots which can cause gastro symptoms and damage the kidneys and other organs. Illustration: JPW and ASPECT Studios Sydney Plans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government intervention State planning minister declares project ‘state significant’, wresting approval process away from local council Penry Buckley Thu 8 Oct 2026 22.02 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 19.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Plans for a grand new public square in the centre of Sydney are in doubt after the New South Wales planning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney. The lord mayor, Clover Moore, released renders in August for the plaza opposite Sydney’s town hall. The design for the space, which the council had expected to be completed by 2031, include a semi-circular clearing projecting eastwards towards Hyde park, with a fountain and a grove of native trees. View image in fullscreen Artists render of the proposed Sydney Town Square redevelopment. Illustration: JPW and ASPECT Studios The plans have been the source of a battle between Moore and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, who has said he does not support the project, describing it as “too expensive, majorly disruptive for Sydney”, and said it would close down businesses in the area. It had also become a flashpoint in a culture war, ridiculed in the Sydney tabloid The Daily Telegraph, which published AI-generated images of the new square heaving with protesters . The council led by Moore, who’s been the city’s progressive independent mayor since 2004, has previously received negative coverage from the publication for other proposals, i ncluding an Oxford Street cycleway first formally raised by the council in 2020. The council has now acquired the last of seven buildings needed to be bulldozed for the square. The demolition and construction was expected to cost $150m. But on Friday, the planning minister, Paul Scully announced he had declared the project a state significant development (SSD), after seeking advice from the NSW Independent Planning Commission, taking the decision for approval away from the council. “This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application,” he said. The project has also been opposed by Woolworths, whose town hall store occupies one of the buildings that would be demolished under the plan. At a press conference outside the store on Friday, the Australian Retail Council’s chief executive, Chris Rodwell, welcomed Scully’s decision. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Look at this building. This is not a building that needs to be bulldozed … it’s home to Australia’s single busiest supermarket.” Scully said the IPC would make the determination on any proposal submitted by the City of Sydney. Under the SSD pathway, the planning minister himself is the consent authority, unless the IPC is delegated to take on that role. In a surprise statement on Friday, Moore, also welcomed the decision to declare the project state significant, saying, “I could not agree more”. “Regardless of who assesses it, we remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported. “The city owns the buildings, has responsibly saved the money over a 40-year period to deliver the project debt free, and has had some of the world’s leading designers and architects work on the plans.” She said the government had recently approved the acquisition of the final property required for the square. But she said the timing of Scully’s intervention “raises questions” and it would be “deeply disappointing” progress was delayed until after the March state election. Moore called on the minister to commit to “a transparent, genuine, fair and impartial assessment” that did not delay the project. Scully declined to comment. In its advice, the IPC noted the project involved “complex interfaces with state-owned transport infrastructure and requires coordinated assessment of engineering, construction, operational and stakeholder issues”. But it said the proposal would “deliver public benefits through the provision of significant civic and social infrastructure”, and had “the potential to generate significant economic benefits through increased tourism, events, cultural activity and visitation to Sydney’s CBD”.
